Collinsia verna is a delicate eastern North American native wildflower that carpets rich floodplain and cove forests in mid-spring with two-toned flowers — a white upper lip and vivid blue lower lip — held in tiered whorls up slender stems, blooming alongside Virginia bluebells and trout lily. It completes its life cycle quickly, flowering, setting seed, and dying back by early summer, so it is best naturalized in a woodland garden where it can self-sow into open patches of leaf litter year after year rather than planted as a permanent bedding annual. Avoid heavy mulch that would prevent the tiny seeds from reaching bare soil, and let plants stand until seed has fully dispersed before any cleanup.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; star chickweed spreads gently to form a low, semi-evergreen mat and is a well-behaved native alternative to common lawn chickweed for a woodland groundcover.

Stellaria pubera is an Appalachian and southeastern native forming loose mats of small, pointed, deep green leaves studded in early to mid spring with clean white, deeply notched, star-shaped flowers that stand out against the darker foliage. It naturalizes readily along shaded slopes and woodland paths, filling in as a low, textural groundcover among trillium, spring beauty, and other native ephemerals without becoming aggressive like its introduced weedy relative. It tolerates typical woodland soil conditions with little maintenance and can be divided in fall to expand the planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Pumila' spreads by stolon into a dense, low groundcover rather than staying in a tight clump like most astilbe cultivars, and blooms later in the season than taller Chinese astilbe selections.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; 'Pumila' spreads by stolon into a dense, low groundcover rather than staying in a tight clump like most astilbe cultivars, and blooms later in the season than taller Chinese astilbe selections. This dwarf Chinese astilbe selection forms a low, spreading mat of finely cut, dark green foliage topped in late summer by upright, fuzzy, lilac-pink plumes that appear after most other astilbes have finished blooming, extending the shade border's flowering season. Its low, groundcover habit makes it useful for edging shaded paths, filling in beneath taller shrubs, or massing as a flowering lawn substitute in consistently moist shade where turfgrass will not grow. Astilbe chinensis selections tolerate more sun and drier soil than other astilbe species, but 'Pumila' still performs best with regular moisture and appreciates a yearly topdressing of compost.

Chrysogonum virginianum var. australe is the stoloniferous, heat-tolerant form of green-and-gold found from the Carolinas through the Gulf Coast, producing the same cheerful, five-petaled, bright yellow, daisy-like flowers over semi-evergreen, hairy, heart-shaped leaves from spring into fall, but spreading more quickly by runners into a loose mat rather than a tight clump. Its greater heat and humidity tolerance makes it a better performer than the typical clumping variety in warm-climate gardens, where it is widely used as a flowering groundcover under high-canopy shade, along woodland paths, and edging shaded beds. It tolerates more sun than most shade groundcovers if soil moisture is adequate, and spreads readily enough that divisions can be shared or used to fill in new areas within a season or two.

directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; mountain bellwort is smaller and more compact than the larger-flowered Uvularia grandiflora, making it a good choice for tucking into tight spots in a woodland rock garden. Uvularia puberula is a compact southeastern native bellwort found on rocky, acidic slopes and forest edges, forming a low clump of glossy, perfoliate leaves with small, twisted, pale yellow, bell-shaped flowers dangling from the stem tips in mid-spring, followed by three-angled seed capsules. Its diminutive scale and tolerance of drier, rockier soil than other bellworts make it well suited to a shaded rock garden or the front of a woodland border alongside foamflower and dwarf sedges. It spreads slowly by rhizome and is best left undisturbed once established, since plants take time to recover from transplanting.
